newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian economy expands at robust pace.
newsitem.headline: Indian economy expands at robust pace.

text.p: India's economy is forecast to expand by a robust 6.8 percent in the fiscal year ending in March, the government said on Thursday in a report that gave a boost to Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.

The Planning Ministry said gross domestic product (GDP), adjusted for inflation, was projected to grow by 6.8 percent in the 1996/97 fiscal year ending on March 31. Earlier unofficial projections had put the rate at about six percent.

The stronger-than-expected growth rate came as welcome news to the government before it tackles the budget for the 1997/98 fiscal year starting on April 1. "This is good news," said H.L. Somany, president of the Associated Chambers of Commerce.

Deve Gowda, thrust into power last June at the head of a centre-left coalition following inconclusive general elections, has been under pressure from political opponents and some industrialists who have complained of an economic slowdown.
A government spokesman drew solace from the relatively strong GDP growth figure, which he said compared favourably with 7.1 percent growth in 1995/96.
"The economy is moving in the right direction," he said. "Growth this year is very, very encouraging."
The prime minister said in December that he would announce measures to stimulate growth and shore up financial markets.
The promises have helped push up share prices on the Bombay Stock Exchange, which have gained some 15 percent since the beginning of the year.
At 1412 GMT on Thursday, the bourse's benchmark index was up virtually unchanged on the day at 3,526.71 points.

Government officials reiterated on Thursday that they did not expect a large package of measures to bolster the capital markets before Deve Gowda and Finance Minister P. Chidambaram leave for the World Economic Forum in Switzerland on Friday.
"There is not any big, one-time package, just a series of measures," a Finance Ministry official said.
The government has announced a string of moves over the past month to spur growth and attract private investment, particularly into the capital-starved infrastructure sector.

On Thursday the Finance Ministry announced that telecommunications companies would be entitled to higher foreign borrowing limits and be offered a tax holiday as well as import duty concessions in early years of operation.
Deve Gowda's cabinet was set to meet on Thursday evening. Authorities said it might consider a welfare package for the rural poor to be presented February 28 in the 1997/98 budget.
A strong rebound in agricultural production is expected largely to offset a slowdown in manufacturing output in the fiscal year ending on March 31, the Planning Ministry said.

Agriculture production, spurred by plentiful monsoon rains, was forecast to grow by 3.7 percent after contracting by 0.1 percent in 1995/96. Manufacturing production was projected to grow by 10.6 percent, down from 13.6 percent in 1995/96.

"The rural area is where the future consumers lie," Somany said. He said greater investment in roads and banks was needed to bring services and goods to rural areas so consumer spending there could stimulate industrial output.
